books.title: The Economic Weapon
books.author: Nicholas Mulder
books.gate: Comparative archival history for readers of international affairs. It explains the origin and use of sanctions; it does not train sanctions practitioners.
reasons: E18/A4: Archival research and several forms of historical evidence support the account. The interwar cases do not identify the independent effect of every sanction.
M15/U14/S12/F7: Trade dependence, finance, deterrence and expectations connect economic pressure to military choices. Strong transfer to supply-chain and strategic-risk analysis.
D7/R9: Substantial institutional detail costs reading time. The interaction of coercion and economic adaptation remains useful beyond current sanctions disputes.
N2/P2: A sustained, careful argument, with more institutional exposition than narrative momentum.
books.theme: International economic and military history. Colonial and humanitarian consequences are part of the causal account, not a predominant excluded theme.
books.concern: Do not turn the interwar record into a universal claim that sanctions always fail or cause war. No serious veto is established; confidence moderate.

books.title: Money Changes Everything
books.author: William N. Goetzmann
refs: IMF review (indexed text; direct access failed)
books.gate: World financial history with sustained explanation of institutions and instruments. This is not investment instruction or a market-reference manual.
reasons: E17/A5: A financial historian links material records and economic interpretation. Sparse ancient evidence limits the certainty of broad causal claims.
M15/U13/S12/F7: Moving value through time, sharing risk and pooling capital link financial contracts to infrastructure, states and trade.
D7/R9: The long historical span reduces density, but the institutional mechanisms are durable.
N2/P2: Accessible for a quantitative reader, though the many episodes make the argument less compact than the best short syntheses.
books.theme: Comparative civilization and finance; neither a single-nation history nor a predominant urban-history account.
books.concern: The title overstates causal reach. Finance can enable a civilization without being its sufficient cause. This reduces E and U; it does not establish a veto.

books.title: A Culture of Growth
books.author: Joel Mokyr
books.gate: An explanatory historical argument across economics, science and culture. Its purpose is not training or technical reference.
reasons: E16/A5: Substantial scholarship and serious specialist debate support authority. Hodgson challenges the weight assigned to exceptional people and the treatment of institutions.
M14/U13/S11/F7: Competition among intellectual communities, political fragmentation and the spread of useful knowledge offer reusable mechanisms.
D7/R9: A long conceptual setup and overlap with Mokyr's other books reduce marginal value. The historical questions remain durable.
N2/P2: The framework is cumulative but sometimes abstract and slow.
books.theme: European comparison with China, focused on the origins of sustained growth.
books.concern: Culture and institutions are difficult to separate causally. The criticism supports a lower evidence score, not a finding of ideological capture or demonstrated central falsity.

books.title: How the World Became Rich
books.author: Mark Koyama; Jared Rubin
books.gate: A short synthesis and argument for general readers, not an economics course text. Use on a reading list does not change its main purpose.
reasons: E17/A4: It compares competing explanations rather than presenting a single cause as settled. Durlauf's review supports the book's nuanced treatment; only its abstract was inspected.
M14/U13/S11/F7: Geography, institutions, culture and population are connected to industrialization. Breadth limits the depth of each mechanism.
D9/R9: A compact route through a large literature; useful as an organizing map even after later research revises details.
N3/P2: Clear sequence and restrained synthesis make it a strong starting point.
books.theme: Comparative global economic development.
books.concern: The book summarizes causal research; it does not resolve identification problems by itself. No veto established. Its score reflects synthesis, not originality.

books.title: The Gifts of Athena
books.author: Joel Mokyr
books.gate: A cross-disciplinary historical explanation organized around useful knowledge, factories and institutions. Some formal analysis does not make its main purpose specialist training.
reasons: E17/A5: A major historian builds a sourced account that has received specialist review. The Varian record establishes scrutiny, not endorsement of unseen arguments.
M16/U14/S12/F7: The relation between knowing why and knowing how, access to knowledge, and resistance to innovation closely matches the requested profile.
D7/R9: Seven connected essays include long excursions, but the knowledge-production mechanisms are durable.
N2/P2: Conceptually disciplined; less effortless to read than trade narrative history.
books.theme: Knowledge, industrialization and institutions dominate. The household-health discussion is one part, not a predominant disease theme.
books.concern: The connection from scientific knowledge to economic performance is historically contingent. Read it as a strong explanatory model, not a complete theory of growth. No veto established.

books.title: The Great Convergence
books.author: Richard Baldwin
books.gate: A sustained explanation of globalization and production networks, not a trade-economics textbook. Its academic language increases difficulty without changing the purpose.
reasons: E17/A5: A specialist in trade develops a historically grounded synthesis. Aggregate trends cannot establish that communication costs explain every relocation.
M15/U14/S12/F7: Separating the costs of moving goods, ideas and people explains why production stages move differently. Excellent transfer to industrial strategy.
D7/R8: Some repetition and forward-looking discussion reduce density and durability relative to the core historical model.
N2/P2: A clear conceptual structure, but dense exposition slows reading.
books.theme: Global production, trade and technology.
books.concern: Predictions about remote services and future integration are scenarios, not current facts. The historical explanation retains value without those predictions; no V4 veto.

books.title: Networks of Power
books.author: Thomas P. Hughes
books.gate: A comparative historical narrative of electrification. The contents connect invention, firms, finance and political institutions; this is not a power-engineering reference or procedure manual.
reasons: E18/A5: Detailed comparative research and a long record of specialist attention give strong support. The retrospective also shows that later scholars have qualified parts of the framework.
M16/U14/S12/F7: Bottlenecks, load balancing, investment and institutional control explain how interconnected systems grow. This is exceptionally close to the requested science-industry-power profile.
D7/R9: Technical and local detail earns much of its length but creates a substantial reading cost. The system-building problems remain durable.
N2/P2: Strong explanatory organization; dense rather than fast.
books.theme: US, British and German systems are compared. City cases explain electrification; urban history is not the predominant purpose.
books.concern: The framework is interpretive, not a validated forecasting law. No serious veto established. This is a better first choice than a general invention catalogue.

books.title: Rescuing Prometheus
books.author: Thomas P. Hughes
books.gate: Four histories of large technical projects, with an explanation of changing coordination methods. It is not a systems-engineering training text.
reasons: E16/A5: A distinguished historian draws together project evidence. The 1998 endpoint leaves the Central Artery project unfinished, which limits conclusions about success.
M15/U14/S12/F7: Coordination, feedback and the boundaries between contractors, scientists and public authorities provide strong strategic transfer.
D7/R8: Four substantial cases earn much of the length. Some conclusions about postwar organizational forms are less durable than the cases.
N2/P2: A coherent comparison, with considerable organizational detail.
books.theme: US projects with international technical and strategic influence. The urban road project is one of four cases; neither urban history nor domestic-only influence predominates.
books.concern: The review questions whether practices in exceptional projects generalize to society. That limits transfer, but does not remove the real mechanisms or establish a veto.

books.title: To Engineer Is Human
books.author: Henry Petroski
books.gate: An explanatory essay with engineering histories for general readers. It does not teach design calculations or train readers to operate a system.
reasons: E17/A5: An engineer and historian uses concrete failures to examine design judgment. A selection of accidents cannot establish a statistical failure law.
M15/U14/S9/F7: Safety margins, extrapolation, assumptions and learning from failure transfer directly to modeling and technical decisions. Finance and geopolitics receive less attention.
D8/R9: A relatively compact treatment of a durable problem; some recurring lessons reduce density slightly.
N3/P2: Memorable cases and clear, controlled exposition.
books.theme: Engineering reasoning is the main subject. Failure cases do not form a predominantly American-tragedy narrative.
books.concern: Success can also teach and failure can mislead. The strongest reading is a critique of untested assumptions, not a claim that failure is necessary for every advance. No veto established.

books.title: Success Through Failure
books.author: Henry Petroski
books.gate: A sustained argument about design change, illustrated by objects and failures. It is not a design-method workbook or an instruction manual.
reasons: E17/A5: Expert engineering knowledge and historical cases support the account. The central claim is an interpretive principle, not a universal causal law.
M14/U13/S9/F7: Dissatisfaction, design constraints and the risks of copying success offer reusable heuristics, with less systemic breadth than Hughes.
D7/R9: Repetition and small-object anecdotes lower density. The basic design questions remain durable.
N3/P2: Clear and memorable prose, with a strong organizing idea.
books.theme: Design and technology across settings.
books.concern: Publishers Weekly treats the failure thesis partly as a device for historical sketches. Read after, rather than immediately alongside, To Engineer Is Human; the overlap reduces marginal value. No veto established.

books.title: Normal Accidents
books.author: Charles Perrow
books.gate: An organizational argument about technology and risk, using case narratives. It is not a safety-engineering textbook or technical reference.
reasons: E13/A5: The book has received sustained specialist attention, including substantial criticism. Hopkins questions the definitions, coverage and validity of the theory; authority does not cancel those objections.
M14/U13/S10/F7: Interaction complexity and tight coupling are useful questions to ask of a system. They are not accepted here as a sufficient model of accidents.
D6/R8: Lengthy cases and the dated Y2K postscript reduce value. The organizational questions remain useful.
N2/P1: The framework is memorable, but broad claims of inevitability reduce precision.
books.theme: Cross-sector and international technology risk, not predominantly environmental or American-tragedy history.
books.concern: V1 is a serious concern. The reviews establish a contested explanatory theory, not a conclusive finding that the whole central account rests on false facts. Retain with low confidence and below the target; do not present it as settled causal science.

books.title: Inviting Disaster
books.author: James R. Chiles
books.gate: Explanatory reporting on accidents and their causes. The survival advice is incidental to the case analysis, not the book's organizing purpose.
reasons: E16/A4: Detailed reporting supports concrete causal chains, but reconstructed cases cannot supply base rates or isolate all counterfactuals.
M15/U13/S10/F7: Schedule pressure, weak signals, human response and component interactions connect technical design to organizations.
D8/R8: A focused collection of cases; some incident explanations may need updating as investigations develop.
N3/P2: Strong case narratives make the general lessons easy to retain.
books.theme: International cases include Bhopal, Chernobyl, Ocean Ranger and Concorde as well as US accidents. The evidence does not establish a predominantly American-tragedy focus.
books.concern: Bill Luckin's specialist review questions the optimistic conclusion about controlling large systems. The cases remain useful without that optimism. No serious veto established.

books.title: Dealers of Lightning
books.author: Michael A. Hiltzik
refs: Kirkus review (contains errors; not used for technical priority claims)
Computer History Museum: Altair fact check
books.gate: A reported history of Xerox PARC and commercialization, not a computing manual or programming text.
reasons: E17/A4: Extensive interviews support the organizational history, while retrospective testimony can favor the participants' explanations.
M14/U14/S11/F7: Research autonomy, business incentives, complementary assets and commercialization explain why invention and value capture diverge.
D7/R9: A long cast of characters reduces density. The institutional mechanisms are useful beyond any particular computer platform.
N3/P2: A readable narrative with a more nuanced business argument than the simple 'Xerox missed everything' story.
books.theme: A research institution with worldwide effects; US location alone does not trigger the deduction.
books.concern: One secondary review wrongly attributes Altair sales to Xerox and blurs invention priorities. Those statements are not accepted as book facts. The more careful PW review distinguishes research success from commercialization; no veto established for the book.

books.title: The Friendly Orange Glow
books.author: Brian Dear
books.gate: A general-audience history of PLATO. Technical passages serve the history rather than specialist skill development.
reasons: E16/A4: Detailed reconstruction preserves evidence from a neglected computing community. Enthusiasm can inflate the importance of priority claims.
M13/U12/S11/F7: Intended educational use, emergent social use and commercialization provide useful mechanisms.
D4/R8: At roughly 640 pages, long anecdotes and backstory impose a large cost. PW explicitly identifies padding and excessive praise.
N2/P1: The narrative is energetic but less controlled and selective than the strongest alternatives.
books.theme: Computing and network communities, not a national-history narrative.
books.concern: PLATO's early features do not prove that later systems descend directly from it. The historical material survives this limit, so no V4 veto; insufficient density keeps it below 80.

books.title: Where Wizards Stay Up Late
books.author: Katie Hafner; Matthew Lyon
books.gate: A narrative history of early networking, not a network-administration or protocol textbook.
reasons: E17/A4: Reported institutional history supports the early-network account. Pioneer interviews can underrepresent competing contributors.
M14/U12/S10/F7: Resource sharing, protocol coordination and public research funding explain how a network becomes usable.
D8/R9: A compact history with durable lessons; some space goes to personalities rather than mechanisms.
N3/P2: Clear storytelling makes the organizational sequence easy to follow.
books.theme: Research infrastructure with international consequences. The US setting alone is not a thematic penalty.
books.concern: It is a history of early development, not a complete account of today's Internet. Avoid reducing origins to either a pure military-survival story or an equally simple denial of all military influence. No veto established.

books.title: Computer Wars
books.author: Charles H. Ferguson; Charles R. Morris
books.gate: An industry history and strategic argument, not a computer-skills manual. Several subtitles identify editions of the same work.
reasons: E14/A4: The industry analysis draws partly on anonymous sources and contemporary judgments. Forecasts require historical framing.
M14/U13/S11/F7: Architecture control, modularity, supplier bargaining and incumbent incentives are transferable.
D7/R6: Some concise analysis is offset by dated industrial-policy forecasts and a post-IBM frame.
N2/P1: Dense and forceful, with less separation between analysis and advocacy than desirable.
books.theme: International computing competition, not domestic-only American history.
books.concern: National competitiveness advocacy and dated predictions reduce E, R and P. The documented architecture mechanisms remain independently useful, so neither V2 nor V4 is established at the serious threshold. Below 80.

books.title: More Money Than God
books.author: Sebastian Mallaby
books.gate: A reported history explaining hedge funds and institutional finance. It does not primarily teach an investment strategy.
reasons: E16/A4: Access and clear financial reporting support the cases. Survivorship and access bias limit the inference from successful managers.
M15/U13/S11/F7: Leverage, incentives, liquidity and differing strategies reveal useful financial mechanisms.
D7/R8: Some personality material and repetition reduce density. The institutional history is more durable than the book's regulatory conclusions.
N3/P2: Clear explanations connect technical trades to a strong narrative.
books.theme: Global markets and financial institutions, not domestic-only influence.
books.concern: PW challenges the favorable claim that hedge funds are safer and less disruptive than banks. Treat that as an argument under dispute, not a settled result. No serious ideological veto established.

books.title: The Power Law
books.author: Sebastian Mallaby
refs: LSE: critical review (indexed text; direct page failed)
books.gate: A narrative history and explanation of venture capital, not a founder or investment training manual.
reasons: E16/A4: Strong access provides rich cases. The LSE review challenges its treatment of economic theory, the state and non-US experience.
M14/U13/S11/F7: Highly uneven returns, staged finance, networks and investor control connect funding to technology development.
D7/R8: Colorful episodes sometimes displace analysis. The historical funding mechanisms outlast individual company valuations.
N3/P2: Clear narrative and explanation, with some overreach in the general framing.
books.theme: International technology finance, including China. The narrative is US-heavy, but its subject and influence are not domestic-only.
books.concern: A few large outcomes do not prove a universal power-law distribution or establish how much value investors caused. These are limits on the thesis, not a demonstrated veto.

books.title: Arms and Influence
books.author: Thomas C. Schelling
refs: Yale book text and contents via JSTOR
books.gate: A public-facing argumentative account of coercion and bargaining, originally linked to public lectures. It is not a specialist mathematical game-theory monograph or military operations manual.
reasons: E16/A5: A major analytical contribution with lasting specialist attention. Historical examples illustrate logic more often than they test its assumptions.
M16/U15/S11/F7: Commitment, credibility, deterrence, compellence and shared risk form a tightly connected strategic model.
D8/R9: High conceptual density with some repeated Cold War examples. The central bargaining problems remain durable.
N3/P2: Clear, precise reasoning makes subtle distinctions memorable.
books.theme: Strategic bargaining across states. Vietnam appears among examples but does not dominate the book.
books.concern: Rational bargaining assumptions can fail under misperception, fragmented authority and different preferences. High utility is conditional on checking those assumptions. No serious veto established.

books.title: The Evolution of Cooperation
books.author: Robert Axelrod
books.gate: An accessible sustained argument from tournaments and historical examples, aimed at readers across disciplines. It is not a course textbook or a programming guide.
reasons: E16/A5: Transparent model assumptions and a large research legacy support authority. A tournament result is conditional on the opponents and rules used.
M15/U14/S9/F6: Repeated interaction, retaliation, forgiveness and the expected future explain how cooperation can become stable.
D9/R9: A compact treatment with durable strategic value, although some formal content will be familiar to a physicist.
N3/P2: Simple models and examples form a clear cumulative argument.
books.theme: General strategic interaction and cooperation across domains.
books.concern: Tit for Tat is not a universally optimal strategy. Later work distinguishes several cooperation mechanisms; the book is a foundation, not a complete current theory. No veto established.

books.title: Micromotives and Macrobehavior
books.author: Thomas C. Schelling
books.gate: A collection of connected explanatory arguments about aggregate behavior, not a course text or specialist methods manual. Models are the means of argument, not a training curriculum.
reasons: E17/A5: The models make assumptions visible. They establish possible mechanisms more securely than the empirical prevalence of those mechanisms.
M16/U14/S10/F6: Thresholds, feedback and unintended aggregate outcomes are highly reusable in simulations, institutional design and strategic thought.
D9/R9: Compact models carry substantial content and remain useful as technology and political actors change.
N3/P2: Concrete examples expose the logic without a heavy formal apparatus.
books.theme: Race and residential sorting are among several applications. The main subject is general aggregation, not racial or urban history; no predominant-theme deduction.
books.concern: An emergent outcome can arise from several different mechanisms. The book should not be used to infer individual preferences from an aggregate pattern alone. No serious veto established.

books.title: The Knowledge Machine
books.author: Michael Strevens
refs: Helliwell: detailed specialist review and edition
books.gate: A trade philosophy-of-science argument using historical cases, not a specialist philosophy monograph or physics textbook. US and UK subtitles differ.
reasons: E14/A4: A qualified philosopher offers a clear thesis, but Helliwell challenges the historical selection and the treatment of probability and scientific reasoning.
M13/U11/S9/F7: Rules of public scientific argument offer an institutional mechanism; the thesis has less marginal novelty for an active theoretical physicist.
D7/R8: Extended setup and historical examples lower density. The institutional question is durable, even if the proposed rule is incomplete.
N3/P2: A readable and conceptually explicit argument, with a provocative framing.
books.theme: Scientific explanation and institutions. Environment is incidental to the closing discussion.
books.concern: The claim that an 'iron rule' largely explains modern science is insufficiently established. The specialist review also contains a factual slip about the location of the omega-minus discovery, so it is not treated as infallible. No conclusive veto; below 80.

books.title: The Most Powerful Idea in the World
books.author: William Rosen
books.gate: A narrative explanation of steam technology and invention. It does not train readers to design or operate engines.
reasons: E15/A3: A researched synthesis by a trade author. The large causal weight assigned to intellectual property needs more testing against competing explanations.
M14/U12/S11/F7: Precision manufacture, experimentation, collaboration and incentives connect inventions to production.
D7/R9: Anecdotes and extended biographies reduce density; the technological constraints remain useful.
N3/P2: A well-organized story with clear technical explanation.
books.theme: History of an invention system and its industrial consequences, primarily in Britain but not a general national history. T0 follows the repo's distinction between technological case history and national history; confidence moderate.
books.concern: The strong patent-centered explanation is a hypothesis, not a settled sufficient cause. At 83, this is a threshold-sensitive recommendation. A broader geography-based reading of the thematic rule would give 73; no other criterion would change.

books.title: The Measure of All Things
books.author: Ken Alder
books.gate: A history of measurement, scientific error and standards, not a surveying manual or technical metrology reference.
reasons: E18/A5: Documentary historical work and specialist attention support the account. It offers a concrete record of measurement practice rather than only a general claim about science.
M14/U12/S10/F7: Error handling, coordination and the adoption of a common standard connect scientific work to trade and state authority.
D7/R9: Travel and personal narrative reduce density; the tension between uncertainty and standardization remains durable.
N3/P2: A clear historical structure makes epistemic problems memorable.
books.theme: The main subject is a scientific measurement project and an international standard, not the general history of France. Revolutionary politics provide constraints; T0 has moderate confidence.
books.concern: The hidden-error narrative can make a standard's origin seem more important than the later ability to reproduce it. The book remains valuable for scientific practice and institutions. Under a broader location-based thematic interpretation, 87 would become 77.

books.title: The Medieval Machine
books.author: Jean Gimpel
books.gate: A popular historical argument, not a technical reference. Original French publication was 1975; the English translation appeared in 1976.
reasons: E12/A3: Both reviews identify weaknesses in the decline framework. Selective statistics and an overextended analogy to modern America reduce confidence.
M12/U10/S10/F7: Energy, agriculture, mining and labor still provide concrete mechanisms of premodern production.
D8/R7: Short and readable, but old scholarship and the speculative historical cycle reduce durability.
N3/P1: Lively exposition; sweeping generalizations reduce conceptual precision.
books.theme: Several European regions and productive technologies. Environmental consequences and a US comparison do not dominate the historical core.
books.concern: V1/V4 are concerns for the framing. Yee explicitly separates the useful historical body from the speculative decline analogy. On that evidence, the book's main descriptive value does not depend on the analogy; retain below 80 with low confidence.

books.title: Cathedral, Forge and Waterwheel
books.author: Frances Gies; Joseph Gies
books.gate: A narrative survey of medieval technology and its diffusion, not a construction or craft manual.
reasons: E16/A4: Established historical synthesis supports the broad account. Specific priority claims and generalizations about ancient stagnation need caution in a work of this age.
M13/U11/S11/F7: Energy conversion, craft skills, agriculture and technology transfer explain cumulative productive change.
D8/R9: A compact survey offers broad content; the durable picture of connected techniques is stronger than any single invention date.
N3/P2: Clear thematic development with concrete examples.
books.theme: Comparative European technology with external influences, not a single-nation history.
books.concern: Less causal depth than Mokyr or Hughes and based on older scholarship. At 84, it is a useful but threshold-sensitive addition. No serious veto established; reader reviews are not used as proof of historical accuracy.

books.title: The Unbound Prometheus
books.author: David S. Landes
refs: Cambridge: book description and second edition
books.gate: A comparative historical explanation of industrial development, not a technical industrial-engineering monograph or course training text.
reasons: E17/A5: A major scholarly synthesis with continuing specialist use. Longstanding influence does not make all older explanations current consensus.
M15/U13/S12/F7: Engineering, enterprise, capital and institutions connect technological change to industrial capacity.
D6/R9: The long survey imposes a large reading cost. The comparative record and productive constraints remain durable.
N2/P2: A sustained argument with dense historical detail.
books.theme: Western European comparison rather than the history of one nation.
books.concern: Read as a major interpretation alongside newer research, not as the last word on global divergence. The linked 2003 second edition updates a book first published in 1969; the embedded antecedent chapter is not counted as the standalone book's first year.

books.title: The Secret of Apollo
books.author: Stephen B. Johnson
books.gate: Borderline checked closely: one reviewer calls it a 'manual', but the actual contents trace historical organizations and compare US and European programs. The publisher quotes a general-reader audience. It explains the origin and consequences of systems management rather than teaching its procedures. Pass, confidence moderate.
reasons: E18/A5: Archival and comparative historical research supports the argument. Specialist reviews identify a substantial contribution within its chosen scope.
M15/U14/S11/F7: Interface control, concurrency and conflicting institutional incentives explain the coordination of complex development.
D6/R9: Considerable administrative detail is a real cost for this reader. It is retained because the detail explains engineering outcomes, not merely offices and names.
N2/P2: An ordered comparison with precise concepts, though less narrative momentum than a trade history.
books.theme: US and European aerospace development, rather than a single-nation story.
books.concern: Systems management is not a universal cure and program outcomes have multiple causes. The institutional mechanisms are sufficiently explicit to pass V3; no other serious veto established.

books.title: Trading and Exchanges
books.author: Larry Harris
refs: Oxford: purpose, original date and detailed contents
books.gate: A market-microstructure textbook and practitioner reference. The contents systematically teach order properties, dealer behavior, spreads, arbitrage and trading strategies; the publisher describes improving traders' performance. Anecdotes and accessible exposition do not change the instructional purpose. Hard exclusion 2 applies before scoring. No score or counterfactual score assigned.

books.title: How Big Things Get Done
books.author: Bent Flyvbjerg; Dan Gardner
books.gate: A mixed explanatory and instructional book whose organizing purpose is to improve the reader's project delivery. Chapters give planning and execution principles; the coda supplies eleven leadership heuristics. Its case histories support that practical training aim. Under this repo's strict rule 2, good evidence and broad usefulness do not exempt it. No score or counterfactual score assigned.
